extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, history, and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, drawn from a historical account of Florence, about constitutional and institutional measures to prevent faction, ambition, and the degeneration of liberty. Emphasizes remedies (laws, a separate executive, restraints on ambition) illustrated by Florence and Rome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power corrupts across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Power has the same effects upon all minds; commons, like kings, nobles, or mobs, when in power discover a disposition to tyrannise over those above and below them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume virtue from social rank; design institutions that check concentration of power in any class. The Florence example shows commons turned tyrannical when they obtained authority, burning houses and committing outrages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make laws stronger than particular persons or families
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a way of making the laws more powerful than any particular persons or families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitute legal structures that limit family- or faction-based domination; ensure laws, not family influence, determine access to offices. The text faults Florence for not contriving a new form that restrains family ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a separate executive (negative/veto) to defend the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate executive, with power to defend itself, is a full remedy against the fatal effects of dissensions between nobles and commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an executive independent of the legislature with negative/defensive powers (veto, enforcement) so that neither branch or faction can monopolize governance. The author notes Machiavelli missed this 'noble invention' and that it would remedy factional contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudent restraint on ambition and customs that nourish faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for constitutions which will restrain the ambition of families; prohibit such customs as tend to nourish and propagate faction, and substitute others that may conduce to maintain liberty and good civil government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prohibitions and civic norms that discourage partisan aggrandizement (e.g., preventing families from monopolizing offices) and cultivate customs that sustain public-spiritedness rather than factionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should serve the common good, not private ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are often made not for the common good but for private ends: laws, statutes, and civil ordinances serve the caprice or ambition of the conqueror, not the true interest of a free people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create checks to prevent victors/factions from enacting self-serving legislation; prioritize institutional safeguards that tie lawmaking to public interest rather than partisan reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on laws, not parties, to support the city
rubrics_metrics.description: A city that endeavours to support itself by parties instead of by laws can never be at peace; when one prevails and is left without opposition, it necessarily divides again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutionalizing party-based governance; strengthen neutral legal processes and impartial magistracies so settlements are durable and not simply temporary partisan victories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial and consistent execution of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the laws themselves may be good and wholesome, partial execution of them affords no remedy; promisses and oaths become meaningless when laws are only partially enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure impartial enforcement and administration of laws; inconsistent application breeds licentiousness and contempt for institutions, increases bribery and impunity, and leads to social decline (as illustrated in Florence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extinguishing civic virtues by wholesale social leveling
rubrics_metrics.description: By depriving nobles of arms and honours and incorporating them with other classes, Florence extinguished the military spirit and greatness of soul which sustained public virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional reforms should preserve channels that cultivate civic and military virtues (honours, duties, responsibilities) rather than eliminating elite roles altogether and thereby removing capacities essential to defence and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the power of private military figures/captains
rubrics_metrics.description: Captains and their adherents were arrogant and dreaded; they were even more dreaded than the signori, and ambassadors were instructed to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject military leaders/mercenary captains to civil control and limit their autonomous authority; otherwise private commanders can become de facto power centers that destabilize the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against leaders disguising pernicious designs as sacred causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ringleaders of parties varnish over their pernicious designs with some sacred title; being enemies to all liberty, they more effectually destroy it by pretending to defend sometimes the rights of the nobility, sometimes of the commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute transparency, accountability, and scrutiny of supposed 'defenders' of rights; scrutinize motives and prevent demagogues from using moral rhetoric to seize power for private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not transfer liberties to foreign rulers out of factional convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: To give that away to others which we could not or would not possess quietly ourselves, we first committed our liberties into the hands of king Robert ... never settling under any government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ceding domestic rights or sovereignty to external princes or powers as a shortcut to settle internal disputes; doing so can result in prolonged instability and loss of self-government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design constitutions to remove root causes (seeds) of division
rubrics_metrics.description: Not one seed had been eradicated: the seeds were in the human heart; constitutions ought to have been contrived so as to produce a remedy for the evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reforming institutions, focus on structural remedies that address underlying incentives (ambition, envy, private aggrandizement) rather than only short-term fixes; otherwise factionalism will recur under new names and actors.
